summary: Sustained small-burst traffic triggers per-customer pacing window causing long-tail stalls and client retry amplification
description:
Issue summary:
Greenline Health reports sudden spikes in perceived inference timeouts and streaming stalls during sustained small-burst traffic patterns. Customer observes long-tail stalls (~10-45s) on a subset of requests, which trigger aggressive client retries and amplify apparent outages.

Impact:
- Multiple customer application endpoints report transient user-facing delays and increased error rates during a 6-hour window on 2026-03-10.
- Estimated 12% of requests from Greenline during the window experienced >10s latency, several timed out client-side before server responded.
- Business impact: mission-critical clinical triage workflows occasionally delayed; customer flagged as P1.

Environment:
- Deployment: Dedicated cluster (Greenline dedicated pool) in us-east-1.
- Models: redwood-v1-large (primary), fallback gpt-open-7B.
- Client: Greenline NodeJS SDK v2.4.1 with default retry backoff.

Steps to reproduce (customer-supplied):
1) Run steady stream of small bursts: 5 requests every 12 seconds per app instance, sustained for 30+ minutes across ~20 app instances.
2) Observe that a small fraction of requests see tokens delayed or the streaming socket pauses mid-response.
3) Client SDK retries after 6s leading to concurrent duplicated requests.

Observed behavior:
- Serving runtime logs show soft per-customer pacing (windowed request pacing) kicking in when burst density exceeds threshold.
- Rate-limiter returns 429 with X-RateLimit-Policy=pacing-window or introduces queueing leading to extended head-of-line blocking for that customer pool.
- Client retries amplify load, causing further queue elongation and increased tail latency.

Expected behavior:
- System should either return a clear 429 quickly or maintain steady short latency for allowed throughput without long queue waits. Client retries should be avoidable when throttling signals are explicit.

Logs & artifacts provided by customer:
- Trace IDs: trace-us-17822a, trace-us-1782ab, trace-us-1782ac (attached).
- Example SDK logs showing retry loop starting at 2026-03-10T14:32:06Z and duplicates created at 14:32:12Z.
- Network capture showing intermittent TCP keepalive during streaming stalls.
comments: 2026-03-10 15:02 - Aisha Patel: Received P1 escalation from Greenline CSM. Customer reporting intermittent long-tail stalls and client retries amplifying the issue. Provided request for traces and SDK logs.

2026-03-10 17:20 - Platform Oncall (Marco Ruiz): Confirmed elevated 429s for Greenline pool in prod/us-east-1 between 2026-03-10T13:40 and 2026-03-10T19:05. Noted concurrent autoscale activity. Collected runtime logs and initial metrics.

2026-03-11 09:40 - Evelyn Chen: Reproduced load profile in staging with a test harness approximating 20 app instances, 5 requests each every 12s. Observed pacing-window enforcement after ~18 minutes with queueing behavior and token-level stalls similar to customer reports.

2026-03-11 13:55 - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Found that pacing-window uses a conservative window-size parameter (0.9 * configured_qps_per_customer) and performs head-of-line queueing instead of rejecting excess quickly. Proposed short-term rule tweak and long-term redesign.

2026-03-12 08:10 - Evelyn Chen: Implemented temporary rule change in a canary (reduce head-of-line queueing window to 0.2s and prefer fast-429) for 10% of traffic; observed reduced tail-latency and fewer duplicate requests from retrying clients.

2026-03-13 11:02 - Greenline (CS contact): Confirmed improvement during the canary window; still seeing occasional stalls when burst pattern exceeds 3x baseline traffic per instance. Requested permanent mitigation plan and guidance for SDK retry settings.
investigation_notes: Hypothesis: Per-customer pacing window algorithm is intended to smooth traffic but currently enqueues excess requests, causing head-of-line blocking and long-tail stalls when client retries occur.
Metrics: During incident window 95th->99.9th percentile latency jumped from 0.9s to 18.4s for greenline pool. 429s increased by 4.6x compared to baseline.
Staging repro: Reproduced queueing behavior deterministically with the customer's burst profile; observed identical pacing-window log markers and queue depth growth.

Root cause analysis: Conservative pacing implementation with long dequeue delay plus SDK default retry timing (6s) creates a feedback loop. Lack of explicit fast-429 for pacing-window allowed retries to pile up instead of failing fast.
Related config: Dedicated pool had custom qps_per_customer cap set lower than assumed by pacing algorithm, misalignment exacerbated head-of-line queueing.
Short-term mitigation validated: prefer immediate 429 (fast-fail) on pacing-window breach; OR surface X-Pacing-Delay header with expected retry-after to clients.

Long-term options: 1) change pacing implementation to token-bucket with immediate rejects beyond capacity; 2) expose clearer throttling headers and SDK changes to respect Retry-After and exponential jitter; 3) autoscale smoothing to absorb short spikes without triggering pacing.
resolution:
Workaround / Temporary fix applied: Deployed canary config (2026-03-12) that converts pacing-window enforcement from head-of-line queueing to immediate 429 for overflowed requests in Greenline's dedicated pool. Observed 70% reduction in client duplicate requests and 80% reduction in 99.9th percentile latency for the canary group.

Permanent remediation plan:
- Short term (next 7 days): Roll out immediate-429 behavior to all dedicated pools with opt-in per-customer exceptions. Publish SDK guidance recommending exponential backoff with jitter and honoring Retry-After headers.
- Medium term (1-2 months): Implement token-bucket style enforcement at the gateway to avoid head-of-line blocking; update telemetry to surface pacing events in Console per-route charts.
- Long term (Q2 roadmap): Add automated detection that adjusts autoscaling headroom for dedicated pools showing sustained bursty patterns and incorporate adaptive pacing thresholds.

Post-incident follow-ups: Confluence runbook updated, PR created (#842) to change pacing behavior, and Customer Success to schedule a technical review with Greenline to review SDK settings and post-rollout verification.
